data.title: Ocasio Cortez: Stevens has 'been with the Republicans' since Congress returned
data.description:
Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.) said Rep. Haley Stevens (D-Mich.) has “been with the Republicans” since Congress returned, after the Michigan Democrat endorsed former Rep. Mike Rogers (R-Mich.) in the midterms.

“She’s been with the Republicans ever since she’s come back … she’s been on the Republican side of the aisle,” Ocasio-Cortez said during an appearance on The Don Lemon Show that aired Thursday.

“This is just the epitome of a certain kind of transactional politics,” she added. “And it’s really sad.”

Stevens’ last-minute endorsement of the Republican candidate in Michigan’s competitive Senate race came after her feud with Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed (D-Mich.). The feud, in the preceding days of the midterm elections, stemmed from a political advertisement tying Israel to high grocery prices in the U.S. Stevens released a statement saying incoming Michigan senator did not condemn the ad forcefully enough.

Rogers lost to El-Sayed last week by over seven points, according to Decision Desk HQ. El-Sayed’s victory in Michigan was one of many Democratic wins in the midterm, with the party flipping GOP-held seats in battleground states like Texas, Kansas, South Carolina, Maine and Iowa.

El-Sayed brushed off Stevens’s endorsement switch, telling reporters, “At the end of the day, I actually don’t think about Haley Stevens.”

Stevens, who has defended her decision multiple times, tripled down on it following the midterm results, saying that her beliefs were “never measured by who would win at the ballot box.”

“I recognize that my decision has consequences. All important decisions do. I don’t regret it, but I am truly sorry that it upset some of my colleagues and people I care about personally,” she said.

Stevens faced significant backlash from her fellow Democrats following her decision and members of her staff resigned shortly after. On Tuesday, former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi (D-Calif.) advised her colleagues against removing Stevens from the House Democratic Caucus before the 120th Congress starts.

Ocasio-Cortez, in her recent interview, said this “isn’t just about endorsing the Republican … this is about a betrayal.”

“It showed that people were right in advocating for Abdul El-Sayed’s candidacy in the primary over someone like Haley Stevens,” the New York Democrat added.

data.title: Merkley, senior Senate progressive, backs Van Hollen over Schumer
data.description:
Sen. Jeff Merkley (D-Ore.), the ranking member of the Senate Budget Committee and an influential progressive voice in the Senate Democratic caucus, announced Friday that he will support Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.) over Sen. Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) to serve as majority leader next year.

“Americans are desperate to restore government by and for the people, not the privileged and powerful. We need leadership that carries that responsibility in their heart and gut. @ChrisVanHollen is that leader,” Merkley posted on X.

“He has my full support for Majority Leader,” he declared.

Merkley, who won re-election last week, came to the Senate in 2009, making him a senior member of the caucus. He is a leading voice on rules reform and rooting special interest money out of politics.

He said that he’s seen Van Hollen “rally support for the people against the powerful time and time again.”

“Politics as usual is unacceptable. The American people have given us the opportunity to deliver. Let’s seize the day and make it happen,” he said.

Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) and Sens.-elect Abdul El-Sayed (D-Mich.) and Peggy Flanagan (D-Minn.) also say they will back Van Hollen for Senate majority leader.

Merkley also announced this week that he will seek the chairmanship of the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee in the next Congress.

Merkley said that as chair of that panel he would prioritize “taking toxics — ranging from asbestos to plastics to forever chemicals — that create significant health problems.

Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse (D-R.I.), who serves as the ranking member of the Environment and Public Works Committee, is set to become chairman of the powerful Senate Judiciary Committee next year.

data.title: Van Hollen calls to abolish Senate filibuster, rules out 2028 White House bid
data.description:
Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.), who is challenging Sen. Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) to be the next Senate majority leader, said on Friday that he wants to abolish the filibuster and ruled out a potential presidential run in 2028.

Van Hollen, speaking to reporters at the What’s Next conference in Denver, argued that legislation should pass the Senate with simple-majority votes and that the filibuster, which requires senators to muster 60 votes to pass most legislation, is “undemocratic.”

“My personal opinion is that we need democracy in the United States Senate and that means allowing ultimately a majority of senators to answer the call of the American people, so that means 51 votes,” Van Hollen said.

“My personal view has been all along that the filibuster is an anti-democratic — small “d” — provision. It’s not in our Constitution. It was put in there by senators to enhance their power over the power of the people,” he added.

“My view is we need to have a system where you have lots of debate, lots of debate, but at the end of the day, a majority reflecting the will of the people should be able to hold a view on an important measure,” he said. “This is an issue that I think we need to talk to the caucus about.”

Van Hollen said filibuster reform is especially important to pass what he called “democracy protection measures” to protect voting rights.

The Maryland senator, who formally announced Thursday his plan to challenge Schumer in a leadership race next month, also said he’s no longer considering a run for president in 2028.

“I’m not running in 2028,” he declared.

Van Hollen told the Hill Nation Summit in July that he was actively exploring a presidential bid.

He visited New Hampshire, an important early presidential primary state, in June and September.

The debate over the future of the Senate filibuster has divided Senate Democrats.

Most Senate Democrats voted for a carve-out of the Senate’s filibuster rule in January of 2022 to advance a democracy reform package that would establish voting protections for minority voters and put in place new campaign finance regulations.

The effort failed because centrist Sens. Joe Manchin (D-W.Va.) and Kirsten Sinema (D-Ariz.) voted against weakening the filibuster rule. Both lawmakers have since left the Senate.

Van Hollen voted for filibuster reform nearly five years ago and Schumer backed it as well.

But Schumer hasn’t said whether the would support scrapping the 60-vote threshold for most bills once Democrats seize control of the Senate next year with at least a 55-seat majority.

data.title: Slotkin: Elected officials fighting over progressive vs. moderate 'missed the plot'
data.description:
Sen. Elissa Slotkin (D-Mich.) said lawmakers who are warring with the opposite faction within the party had “missed the plot” of the midterm results during a major Democratic conference on Friday. 

“I think Michigan gave a really clear demonstration that whatever side of the Democrats you feel like you’re on, that is not what is important right now, OK? Teamwork is what is important,” Slotkin told attendees at the What’s Next conference in Denver, saying people had “voted very clearly for a new generation of leadership.” 

“If you have elected officials who are spending all their time fighting progressive versus moderate, then they have missed the plot of the election,” she continued. “That new generation is not going to be defined by progressive versus moderate. That new generation, quite simply, is are you on Team Fight or are you on Team Flight?” 

Slotkin was among a number of high-profile Democrats who spoke at the party gathering in Colorado this week, which also included House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (N.Y.), Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro and Rep. Ro Khanna (Calif.). 

Slotkin is also considered a potential White House candidate in the next presidential election, and she confirmed to reporters that she was “seriously” considering it. 

“I want to be a part of the next generation of leaders going forward that does things differently and understands who they serve,” she told reporters after leaving the stage.  

“I’m looking at it, I’m looking at it seriously, but I haven’t made any decisions,” she said.  

Other colleagues and party members who are also looking at runs for the White House next cycle who attended the Democratic conference in Denver included Shapiro, Khanna, Sen. Ruben Gallego (D-Ariz.), among others.

data.title: Navy removed naval destroyer commander deployed to Middle East
data.description:
The U.S. Navy removed a commander of the naval destroyer in late September that was deployed to the Middle East in support of military operations against Iran due to “loss of confidence” after had had been in the job for less than a year, The Hill has learned. 

Commander of the Carrier Strike Group Ten, Rear Adm. Todd F. Cimicata, relieved Cmdr. Caitlin Cunningham of her duties as USS Michael Murphy’s commanding officer on Sept. 27, a Navy official told The Hill on Friday. 

Cunningham began her role as the skipper of USS Michael Murphy, an Arleigh Burke-class Aegis guided-missile destroyer, in late October last year before the ship embarked on an 11-month deployment, which ended this week. 

The destroyer departed Pearl Harbor on Dec. 1, 2025, operating alongside flagship Nimitz-class aircraft carrier USS Abraham Lincoln. 

No additional information was available about Cunningham’s removal, which was reported earlier by USNI News. 

Michael Murphy helped enforce the U.S. naval blockade in the Strait of Hormuz, operating in the North Arabian Sea and Gulf of Oman

“The Sailors of Michael Murphy demonstrated unmatched grit, professionalism and warfighting excellence during this deployment,” Cmdr. David Nicolas, Michael Murphy’s commanding officer, said in a press release, “Whether defeating incoming air and surface threats or leading operations through contested choke points, this crew never hesitated.” 

They answered every call of our nation, defended our allies, and lived up to the heroic namesake,” Nicolas said. “I could not be prouder of this crew.”

data.title: Tanker collides with riverboat on Mississippi River at Port of New Orleans
data.description:
NEW ORLEANS (WGNO) – Emergency response crews rushed to the scene of an accident on the Mississippi River on Friday, after a tanker collided with a cruise ship near the Port of New Orleans.

A news release issued by the Port of New Orleans said the American Cruise Lines’ American Heritage riverboat was docked at the port when it was struck by the Atlantic Asphalt tanker at about 12:30 p.m., local time.

At the time of the collision, officials estimated there to be 129 passengers on the American Heritage, along with the boat’s crew.

“Port NOLA Harbor Police, the New Orleans Fire Department, the New Orleans Police Department, the U.S. Coast Guard and emergency medical personnel are on scene, conducting rescue and response operations,” the release said.

A triage area has been set up inside the Port of New Orleans Administration Building, officials added.

Video of the incident shared to social media appeared to show the American Heritage riverboat falling to one side, rapidly taking on water.

This is a developing story.

data.title: House Democrats' campaign arm investigates sexual harassment allegation against Poindexter
data.description:
House Democrats’ campaign arm is investigating Rep.-elect Brian Poindexter (D-Ohio) for an allegation of sexual harassment, the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee (DCCC) confirmed to The Hill Friday.

“The DCCC has been made aware of the allegations and takes them seriously. In the interest of fairness to all parties involved, we have hired an independent, third-party firm to investigate any instance of inappropriate behavior, conduct interviews and gather the facts. Upon completion of that investigation … the DCCC will have further comment,” DCCC executive director Julie Merz said in a statement.

A spokesperson for Poindexter’s campaign said it is aware of the interaction being investigated, and that Poindexter thought he made a harmless comment to a volunteer on his campaign, but later learned how the woman felt.

“Brian gave what he thought was an innocuous compliment to a volunteer. He heard later that it made her feel uncomfortable and he felt awful,” the spokesperson said in a statement to The Hill. “When Brian learned about this, we immediately began to work to get to the bottom of it with an outside HR firm. Neither Brian nor the campaign ever wants anyone to feel uncomfortable.”

Poindexter recently defeated the embattled Rep. Max Miller (R) in the race for Ohio’s 7th District.

Miller was facing allegations of domestic abuse against his ex-wife and young daughter, which he denied. The Ohio Republican’s ex-wife is the daughter of Ohio Sen. Bernie Moreno (R), who at the time the allegations came out said Miller needed “serious psychological help.”

Some Senate Republicans abandoned support for Miller’s reelection bid in solidarity with Moreno. Miller ultimately lost to Poindexter by nearly 10 percentage points in a district President Trump carried by 11 points in 2024.

Poindexter is set to be sworn in with the new Congress Jan. 3.

Politico previously reported that some key Democratic fundraising groups removed Poindexter from their endorsements lists before the allegation emerged.

data.title: DeSantis on defense secretary speculation: 'I've never discussed it' with Trump
data.description:
Outgoing Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis said he has “never discussed” replacing Pete Hegseth as Defense Secretary with President Trump despite recent speculation.

“I see President Trump frequently now that he’s back in Florida, I’ve never discussed it with him. It’s never been anything that I’ve asked,” DeSantis said when asked if he would be interested in replacing the defense secretary during a Fox News podcast interview.  

The calls for Hegseth’s impeachment came as Democrats secured a sweeping victory in the midterm elections, winning key races in battleground states like Texas, South Carolina, Ohio, Iowa and Kansas. The efforts were spearheaded by outgoing Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.) who introduced eight articles of impeachment — accusing the defense secretary of abusing his powers, including during the war in Iran.

On Tuesday, House Republicans voted to shelve the impeachment measure in a tight 211-204 vote, placing a halt on the effort until the next Congress.

Last week, CBS News reported that DeSantis is being floated as a possible replacement for Hegseth’s position citing one unnamed source. A source, however, said the Florida governor is not interested in the role.

Massie, this week, told reporters that DeSantis would be “great” at the job, adding, “he understands the legality and constitutional boundaries between the legislative and the executive branch, so he’d be great at that. But I’m only telling you his name because I think he probably doesn’t want it.”

“I think you can disagree with a cabinet secretary, but to just try to use impeachment on policy grounds and policy difference, I don’t think that that’s a good precedent,” DeSantis said during the interview.

“I think the Republicans were right to say no to that, and I think the President’s right to stand by his secretary and not cave to that type of tactic,” he added.

The president has stood by Hegseth amid the impeachment calls, reaffirming his support and confidence in him during an interview with CBS News’s 60 Minutes, which aired Sunday. In a Truth Social post on Tuesday, the president gave Hegseth an “A” plus for his work at the Pentagon and called Massie “a TOTAL LOSER.”

data.title: Florida city cancels St. Patrick's Day, Pride events ahead of law banning local DEI funding
data.description:
DELRAY BEACH, Fla. (WFLA) — A city in Florida announced this week that it will not host its annual St. Patrick’s Day Parade or Pride event in 2027, crediting the decision to a piece of legislation championed by Gov. Ron DeSantis (R).

DeSantis had signed SB 1134 into law in April, restricting municipal funding, promotion, and official actions involving activities that the law defines as diversity, equity, and inclusion (DEI) as of Jan. 1, 2027. The restrictions include “programming, or activities designed or implemented with reference to race, color, sex, ethnicity, gender identity, or sexual orientation,” according to the bill.

The City of Delray Beach, in messages posted to Facebook and its St. Patrick’s Day parade website, said it believed the Pride and St. Patrick’s Day parades violate these stipulations.

“Following a review of the legislation and its requirements, the City has determined that it is legally prohibited from organizing, funding, or promoting these events in 2027,” a Facebook message posted to the city’s official page reads.

The post shared to the city’s St. Patrick’s Day parade website, meanwhile, says the parade can go on as planned if it’s not funded or planned by the city, but rather private entities or individuals. On his own Facebook page, Carney said the city is now “working feverishly with multiple entities” to put the parade back on.

Carney did not mention whether Delray Beach is also working with sponsors to put on its Pride festivities. But he reportedly said he would support private funding for the Pride parade as well, local outlet CBS12 reported.

In the meantime, Delray Beach officials said the legislation still allows for celebrations of federal holidays (of which St. Patrick’s day is not) and could continue to plan for such events.

“We remain committed to serving all residents and providing opportunities for community engagement consistent with applicable state and federal laws,” the St. Patrick’s Day parade site reads.

DeSantis, responding to a news article on Delray Beach’s decision, claimed on X that the city is engaging in “malicious compliance.”

“What they are doing is not mandated by Florida law. It’s just an attempt to make a political point — a point that legacy media will no doubt try to amplify. We’ve seen these stunts throughout the years. Rinse and repeat,” DeSantis wrote.

Critics, however, promptly pointed out that Delray Beach’s interpretation of SB 1134’s language appeared to be valid, no matter the reasoning for their choice to obey the law.

“The best way to get rid of a bad rule/law is to follow it,” one X user wrote. “Today’s lesson: Don’t create stupid rule/laws.”

data.title: Boebert ousted by Laubacher in Colorado House race
data.description:
Democrat Eileen Laubacher is projected to win Colorado’s 4th Congressional District, according to Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ).

Laubacher defeated incumbent Rep. Lauren Boebert (R-Colo.), unseating one of President Trump’s most outspoken allies in a district that has long favored the GOP. DDHQ rated the seat “likely Republican” heading into Election Day.

The Democrat notched 48.8 percent of the vote while the incumbent garnered 47.8 percent, with over 95 percent of the vote tallied as of Friday.

The victory cuts short Boebert’s congressional career after six years on Capitol Hill, including a controversial district switch that helped her secure a third term in 2024.

The Colorado Republican first arrived in Washington in 2021 after winning the state’s 3rd District, quickly establishing herself as a prominent figure in the House GOP’s conservative wing. But her political fortunes became increasingly uncertain in 2022, when she narrowly survived a challenge from Democrat Adam Frisch by only 546 votes.

Rather than face another potentially difficult reelection fight, Boebert announced in late 2023 that she would run in the 4th District, which was being vacated by retiring GOP Rep. Ken Buck.

The move paid off, and she won the seat in 2024 by roughly 12 percentage points, securing another two years in Congress.

This time, however, she faced a well-funded challenge from Laubacher, a retired two-star Navy admiral and former GOP member who made her military background and national security experience central to her campaign.

The Democrat spent 34 years in the Navy, including assignments in Afghanistan and India, and later served on the National Security Council in former President Biden’s administration. She also built a significant fundraising advantage, bringing in millions more than Boebert during the campaign, Federal Election Commission filings show.

Laubacher emphasized affordability, healthcare and fiscal responsibility, while criticizing Trump’s tariffs and the administration’s handling of the war with Iran.

Boebert, meanwhile, leaned into her support for Trump’s agenda, particularly on immigration and border security.
